parts.layout_phase: Period II (Mature Harappan), its first structural phase: 'Phase 1' of five tentative Mature Harappan levels in Nath 1998; 'phase-IV', the first phase of Period II, in Nath 2014
parts.what_was_built: A mud-brick fortification wall around the mound, first built at the start of the Mature Harappan occupation, and inside it a grid of streets and lanes with podiums, a granary and drains. In the gateway cuttings Nath (1998: 43) gives the wall a thickness of 5 m in Phase 1; a burnt-brick buttress was added in Phase 2, the thickness was doubled and an entrance stair built in Phase 3, the top was paved with burnt brick between guard cells in Phase 4, and mud-brick courses raised it in Phase 5, while 'a lane parallel to fortification walls remained undisturbed till the last occupation at the site'. The 2014 report states that the 'fortification wall of phase-IV' was 'reconstructed in phase-V', with two circular hearths of Period I, Phase II beneath it, and that the inhabitants 'built the enormous mud brick platform and granary in the phase-V' (Nath 2014: 118). It describes 'streets and lanes joined in a chess board pattern' (p. 95) and says 'the period II people follow his predecessor plan and did not change more on city plan' (p. 113). Nath 1999: 48 describes the wall as a mud-brick core with burnt-brick facing inside and out, and the 1999-2000 season exposed a western stretch 12 m wide with a stepped entrance of burnt brick (IAR 1999-2000: 32). Public drains appear 'from the lower-middle phase' (Nath 1998: 43).

(p. 4). The preliminary reports of 1998-2001 in Puratattva and Indian Archaeology: A Review give no dates.

syntheses.statement: Reprints twelve BSIP determinations from RGR-1, RGR-2 and RGR-6 supplied by Nath, without period or phase, and states that the excavations 'revealed all the phases of the Harappan civilization, i.e., period I (Early Harappan), period II (Mature Harappan) and period III (Late Harappan)'.
syntheses.disagreement: Nath's own reports found no Late Harappan deposit in the stratified cuttings of RGR-1 and RGR-2 (Nath 1999: 46; Nath 2014: 104), and ten of Dikshit's twelve laboratory numbers do not appear in Nath's 2014 table.

parts.conflicts: The phase in which the wall was first built is numbered differently in the two main accounts: Phase 1 of five Mature Harappan levels in the 1998 interim report, which warns that 'the present observations would be subject to correction' until trenches across the wall were verified, and phase IV of a Period II divided into phases IV to VI in the 2014 report. Both put the first wall at the beginning of the Mature Harappan occupation. Reported widths differ by location and season: 5 m in Phase 1 at the gateway (Nath 1998: 43), 12 m for the western stretch (IAR 1999-2000: 32) and a maximum breadth of 6 m at the north-western corner (Nath 2014: 111). Among the radiocarbon determinations, BS-3323 in Dikshit's table comes from the same depth (8.45 m) as Nath's Early Harappan BS-3324 but gives 3910 ± 100 against 5200 ± 100, and its printed calibrated age is impossible for its radiocarbon age. No determination is tied to the wall itself or to a named structural phase.

parts.layout_phase: Period I (Early Harappan), structural phase 2 (IAR 1998-99; 'phase II', sub-phases IIa and IIb, in Nath 2014), within sub-period I(b) 'formative urbanism'; Nath 1999 numbers the same planned phase 'Phase-I'
parts.what_was_built: The first planned layout on RGR-1 belongs to the Early Harappan period. Of three Early Harappan structural phases, the second 'revealed the beginning of planned settlement', with a public drain lined with burnt brick, a house drain joining it, houses aligned on either side and a courtyard paved with burnt-brick bats sloping towards the drain (IAR 1998-99: 13; Nath 2014: 104, 115, 118, which speaks of 'a genius planning of ... street with nullah'). The 2014 report characterises Period I(b) as an 'organized settlement where in structures were laid parallel to streets running at right angle, besides developing the concept of public drainage system' (p. 129), and states that after a flood ended Period I, phase III, the Period II settlers 'also followed the phase III plan' (p. 105). In Period II the mound carried streets 1 to 3 around house complexes and a lapidary workshop (pp. 113, 115-117); in the 1997-98 cutting G6 the Mature Harappan structural phases 1 to 4 were 'aligned, on either side, to a lane (1.50 m wide)', and those of phase 5 'were not in exact alignment' (IAR 1997-98: 55-57; Nath 1998: 42). No peripheral wall was found around RGR-1 in Period I (Nath 2014: 114).

syntheses.statement: Summarises Period I at Rakhigarhi as three structural phases with drainage systems, a courtyard floor, circular pits and fire chambers, and lists six further BSIP determinations from RGR-1 without phase.

parts.conflicts: The planned Early Harappan phase is 'phase-2' in IAR 1998-99: 13 and phase II in Nath 2014: 104 and 115, but 'Phase-I' in Nath 1999: 47, which describes the same drain and courtyard. The thickness of the Early Harappan deposit is 'nearly two and a half metre' in IAR 1998-99: 13, 'nearly three metres' in Nath 1999: 47 and 4 m of the 6 m deposit in Nath 2014: 94. Nath's only Early Harappan date from this mound (BS-3344) has no depth. Dikshit's table prints field sample No. 43 twice at the same depth with ages of 5230 ± 90 (BS-3314) and 3810 ± 70 (BS-3353); both cannot belong to one sample.

parts.layout_phase: Period I(b), formative urbanism (structural phases 4 to 6 in IAR 1999-2000; the 2014 report singles out phase V)
parts.what_was_built: On RGR-6 the excavators found Early Harappan houses on either side of a street 1.92 m wide, laid out in Period I(b) over rectangular houses of Period I(a) whose walls 'were running right across the cutting of street'. The street was kept through three successive structural phases: in phase 4 a room built of sun-dried bricks of 3:2:1 ratio, in phase 5 a house of two rooms and a courtyard beside a lane 92 cm wide, with the same layout partly exposed across the lane, and in phase 6 rooms within enclosure walls on both sides of the street (IAR 1999-2000: 30-31). The 2014 report says phase V 'give a clear picture of planning settlement of early Harappan folk' with 'a good network of street and lane' and a house complex of seven rooms opening onto them (Nath 2014: 122). Early Harappan occupation at RGR-6 ended with the start of Period II (p. 129).

parts.part: RGR-4 and RGR-5 (southern mounds under Rakhi Khas and Rakhi Shahpur)
parts.layout_phase: Period II (Mature Harappan); no structural phase stated
parts.what_was_built: Before excavation Nath (1998: 41) recorded in a cliff section on the south-western part of the combined mound 'a massive mud-brick fortification wall with successive mushtika beddings, overlain by successive mud-floors', with a burnt-brick drain beside it, and took 'the evidence of fortification wall from RGR2, 3 and 4' as a sign of 'individual habitation-zones within an integrated network of town planning'. Excavation in 1998-2000 found only Mature Harappan remains on RGR-4 and RGR-5 (IAR 1999-2000: 30): a trench on RGR-4 was opened to see whether the fortification extended onto it (Nath 1999: 46), RGR-4 gave 'structural evidence of platforms and streets' (Nath 2001: 45) and RGR-5 gave bone and ivory working. A cutting on RGR-4 traced a large podium first seen at the south-eastern corner of RGR-2 (Nath 2014: 96).

parts.part: whole town (Mature Harappan city, RGR-1 to RGR-5)
parts.what_was_built: The excavator treats the integrated mounds RGR-1 to RGR-5 as one planned Mature Harappan city and divides it 'into citadel, middle town and lower town' (Nath 2014: 93), naming only RGR-2 as the citadel. He infers that 'the Harappans must have prepared a blueprint of the proposed town before providing all the civic amenities', citing platforms, streets and drains, public wells, separate industrial areas, houses in rows, 'fortification walls of uniform width', the granary and the podiums (p. 103), and states that the Period II settlers 'followed the phase III plan' of the Early Harappan town (p. 105).

syntheses.statement: Reports that AMS dates for charcoal 'from different depths at the Rakhigarhi site' at 9.1 and 20.6 m 'yielded calibrated dates of 2273±38 years BCE and 2616 ±73 years BCE, respectively', citing Vahia et al. 2016.
syntheses.disagreement: Vahia et al. 2016: 28 give 2762 ± 73 BC for the 20.6 m sample, and their table gives 2762-2470 BC and 4616 ± 73 BP for it; 2616 matches none of these.

syntheses.statement: Places the Rakhigarhi cemetery (RGR-7) in 'the Mature Harappan period, date-estimated to 2,500–2,000 BCE'.
syntheses.disagreement: Not tied to the town's layout; it is a period estimate for the cemetery.

syntheses.page: Introduction and STAR Methods, 'Contextual date for individual I6113' (PMC HTML without page numbers)
syntheses.statement: States that 'seven dates from charcoal at depths of 9–23 meters have point estimates of 2800–2300 BCE, which largely fall within the mature phase of the IVC', and that these come from 'the main habitation area'.
syntheses.disagreement: Vahia et al. 2016 publish no mound and a deepest sample of 20.6 m, and their own maximum ages run from 2351 to 2780 BC rather than to 2800 BCE.

syntheses.statement: In a regional summary for the Ghaggar basin sites including Rakhigarhi, gives the Early Harappan as 6000–2600 BCE and the Mature Harappan as 2600–1900 BCE, divided into periods IIA and IIB (2600–2400 BCE) and IIC (2200–1900 BCE) 'on the basis of a few accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) dates', and says that streets and drainage systems appear 'from period IIA on'.
syntheses.disagreement: This later excavator's scheme starts the planned Mature Harappan phase about 2600 BCE and the Early Harappan about 6000 BCE; Nath places the Early Harappan formative stage in the 4th millennium BCE and the first occupation in the 5th, and his Period II dates are calibrated ages of 4560 and 4320 yrs BP. The summary does not say which dates or which site support each boundary.

parts.conflicts: The two dated series cannot yet be joined: Nath's BSIP dates are tied to periods but come from three mounds with few depths, while the IUAC AMS series of Vahia et al. has depths but no mound, trench or phase. Later papers by the Deccan College team restate the AMS results inconsistently (2616 BCE in Shinde et al. 2018; 2800–2300 BCE over 9–23 m in Shinde et al. 2019).

first_occupation.phase: Period I(a), pre-formative urbanism (Early Harappan), at RGR-6 and RGR-1; Appendix 2 of the 2014 report calls it the 'Sothi Phase'
first_occupation.basis: Radiocarbon. Two BSIP determinations from RGR-6 (BS-3318, 5640 ± 110 BP; BS-3341, 5440 ± 290 BP), whose calibrated values the report gives as 6420 ± 110 and 6230 ± 320 yrs BP (Nath 2014: 57, 129). The report assigns the pre-formative stage to 'circa 5th millennium BCE' (p. 76), which we entered as [5000, 4000]. Natural soil was not reached at RGR-6 (IAR 1999-2000: 30), so occupation may begin earlier there; on RGR-1 the Early Harappan deposit 'shows the beginning of occupation over the alluvium' (IAR 1998-99: 13).

notes:
Rakhigarhi is a cluster of mounds. RGR-1 to RGR-5 form the integrated city, RGR-6 (Arda) is a separate Early Harappan mound and RGR-7 is the Mature Harappan cemetery; the Deccan College volume of 2023 lists newly discovered localities RGR-8 and RGR-9, which no excavation report we found describes. Our account of the layout rests on the ASI excavations of 1997-2000 directed by Amarendra Nath, which we read in three forms: the season reports in Indian Archaeology: A Review for 1997-98 to 1999-2000, the interim articles in Puratattva 28, 29 and 31, and the draft final report of 2014 held by the Internet Archive. Nath divides the occupation into Period I (Early Harappan), split into I(a) 'pre-formative urbanism' and I(b) 'formative urbanism', and Period II (Mature Harappan). The 2014 report numbers the structural phases continuously, I to III in Period I and IV to VI in Period II, while the interim reports number phases afresh within each period and mound, so the same phase can carry different numbers. Planned layouts appear twice: Early Harappan streets and drains on RGR-1 and RGR-6 in Period I(b), and the fortified citadel on RGR-2, with its street grid, podiums and granary, at the start of Period II, when the excavator says the settlers kept the earlier plan.

The dating evidence is thin. Nath's 2014 table lists six determinations from the Birbal Sahni Institute (BSIP) with periods, and Dikshit (2022) prints twelve BSIP determinations from the same excavation without periods; only two laboratory numbers overlap, and the tables disagree about field sample No. 51. Neither source states the half-life or the calibration curve, and both head a column 'Calibrated Age (Yrs BP)' without saying how it was computed, so we left half_life_printed and the 5568-year fields null for these dates. The Birbal Sahni Institute lists published in Radiocarbon in 1978-1982 used the conventional 5570-year half-life, but that does not establish the convention for these later measurements. The seven AMS dates of Vahia et al. (2016) come from a 2015 Deccan College trench whose mound and phases are unpublished, so we filed them under the whole town. No determination is tied to the construction of a wall, street or platform, and no Bayesian model of phase boundaries has been published for Rakhigarhi. Determinations from later phases are included only where the source gives no phase, because we cannot then exclude them.

Sources sought and not obtained: the Deccan College report on the 2013-2016 habitation excavations (Shinde, Shin and Bhattacharyya (eds) 2023, New Perspectives on the Harappan Culture in Light of Recent Excavations at Rakhigarhi: 2011-2017, vol. 1, chapter 3, 'Excavations 2013-2016', pp. 43-63), of which only the publisher's sample with the front matter and chapter 1 is open; its list of figures shows trenches on RGR-2, RGR-4 and RGR-6. The IUAC date list I (Sharma et al. 2020, Radiocarbon 62(5), doi:10.1017/RDC.2020.44) is paywalled, and its open abstract page names Rakhigarhi only in a reference. We found no report of the ASI excavations of 2021-2024, only press articles, which we did not use. Indian Archaeology 2011-12 is not online at the address that holds the other volumes, and Indian Archaeology 2012-13 (saved at data/raw/2026-10-21-town-axes/dating/rakhigarhi/iar2012-13.pdf) has no Rakhigarhi excavation entry. We did not consult Possehl's compilations of 1999 and 2002; the first Rakhigarhi determinations we found in print date from 2014. Page 44 of Nath 2001 is largely illegible in the scan, and IAR 1999-2000: 31-32 carries the same season's account. The ASI Chandigarh Circle inventory of protected monuments held locally (data/raw/2026-10-06-evidence-census/sites-deep/c-north-india/rakhigarhi_inventory.pdf, entry 33) gives no dates. Nath 1998: 41 also reports, from a cutting made by villagers on RGR-3, courses of burnt brick and mud brick side by side that he takes to be 'two phases of construction in the fortification wall'; RGR-3 was not excavated, and no phase is given.
